When the data is not binary, it is forcefully binarized using a one-versus-the-rest simplification. In this work, we discuss the limitations of existing metrics and propose novel, mathematically sound, and generalized multi-group and multi-class formulations of the metrics. Ultimately, our results highlight the empirical assessment distortion caused by binarization strategies, which reveals the limitations of binary fairness metrics in the multi class setting.
Machine Learning.comment: Submitted to ACM Transactions on Intelligent Systems and Technology (TIST)

Machine Learning.title: Poisson Super Learning For Survival And Competing Risks On A Discretized Time Scale
Machine Learning.summary: We introduce the Poisson Super Learner, a scalable ensemble method for survival and competing risks prediction with right-censored data. The approach exploits the correspondence between the likelihood of piecewise-constant hazard models and the Poisson likelihood. After expanding the data over a chosen time partition, candidate hazard learners are trained under a common Poisson loss, and cross-validated log-hazard predictions are combined by a Poisson meta learner. The resulting ensemble is a geometric combination of candidate hazards, and can be used to estimate survival probabilities and cause-specific absolute risks. The Poisson Super Learner framework is modular and can in principle incorporate any learner that can estimate interval-specific hazards, including parametric, penalised, additive, and other machine-learning hazard models. Training targets the cause-specific hazard directly and does not require explicit modelling of the censoring distribution. For competing risks, separate cause-specific ensembles are fitted and subsequently combined to obtain individualised cumulative incidence predictions. We illustrate the approach using data from the Steno Diabetes Center collected between 2005 and 2022 to predict cardiovascular disease risk in patients with type 1 diabetes from detailed covariate information. The applied analysis is complemented by simulation studies designed to reflect key features of the data and to examine the behaviour of the method under controlled settings. All analyses were implemented using the freely available R software package poissonsuperlearner.

Machine Learning.title: Anomaly-ranked confirmation slows new-class learning
Machine Learning.summary: Anomaly detectors rank unfamiliar examples for expert confirmation, and the confirmed examples teach a classifier to recognise a new class. Across five benchmarks from physics, medicine and computer vision, the members flagged by the detector are those the classifier learns first. In three systems, confirming the highest-ranked members of a new class gives lower recognition than confirming the same number of random members. Handing subsequent selection to the promoted classifier recovers part of this loss in two systems. A paired intervention further shows that replacing nearby known classes with distant ones sharply reduces the confirmations needed for recognition. These results distinguish finding a new class from selecting examples that teach its extent: within the tested classes, concentrating confirmations at the top of the anomaly ranking makes learning less efficient.

Machine Learning.title: Bolek: A Multimodal Language Model for Molecular Reasoning
Machine Learning.summary:
Molecular property models increasingly support high-stakes drug-discovery decisions, but their outputs are often difficult to audit: classical predictors return scores without rationale, while language models can produce fluent explanations weakly grounded in the input molecule.
  We introduce Bolek, a compact multimodal language model that grounds natural-language reasoning in molecular structure by injecting a Morgan fingerprint embedding into an instruction-tuned text decoder. Bolek is fine-tuned on molecular alignment tasks, including molecule description, RDKit descriptor prediction, and substructure detection, and on downstream reasoning over 15 TDC binary classification tasks using synthetic chains-of-thought anchored in concrete molecular features.
  Across these tasks, Bolek outperforms its Qwen3-4B-Instruct base on all endpoints in yes/no mode and on 13 of 15 in chain-of-thought mode, raising mean ROC/PR AUC from 0.55 to 0.76. It also outperforms TxGemma-9B-Chat on 13 of 15 binary classification tasks despite being less than half its size. Bolek's explanations are more grounded than those of the baseline LLMs: it cites numerical descriptors 10-100x more often per chain-of-thought, and the cited values agree strongly with RDKit for key descriptors such as TPSA, MolLogP, and MolWt (Spearman rho = 0.87-0.91). Generalisation extends beyond the training panel: on 15 unseen TDC classification endpoints, Bolek matches TxGemma on five, and it produces non-trivial rank correlations on three held-out regression endpoints despite never seeing downstream regression during training.
  These results suggest that targeted modality injection and reasoning supervision tied to verifiable molecular features can yield compact, auditable molecular reasoning models.

Machine Learning.title: A Common Language for Dynamic Graphs: Interaction Tokenization Enables Foundation Models
Machine Learning.summary: Dynamic graphs capture evolving interactions in Web systems, including online communication, user engagement, and recommendation. Graph foundation models aim to reuse predictive capabilities across networks, but extending this capability to dynamic graphs faces two challenges. First, node identities are graph-specific, and similar interaction patterns can appear at different temporal and activity scales, making histories difficult to represent consistently across networks. Second, the predictive roles of historical patterns vary across interaction dynamics, limiting transfer from a narrow range of training processes. In this paper, we show that a common interaction language, combined with learning across diverse interaction processes, offers a basis for dynamic graph foundation modeling. We propose CL-DGFM, a Common Language Dynamic Graph Foundation Model for temporal link prediction. Its Dynamic Interaction Tokenizer encodes interaction memory, historical connectivity, and ordered destination transitions into calibrated tabular inputs, making dynamic histories accessible to existing predictors without an additional trainable graph encoder. Its Dynamic Interaction Prior trains a pretrained tabular foundation predictor across diverse synthetic dynamics. Labeled historical context guides prediction, with a Contextual Value Adapter modulating attention values. The model transfers to real graphs without target-graph parameter updates. Experiments on TGB and TGB-Seq demonstrate competitive performance. Further comparisons show that the common language supports basic machine learning and neural models, and enables direct use of frozen tabular foundation models on dynamic graphs.

Machine Learning.title: Forecasting How RLHF Responds to Reward-Model Edits Before Training
Machine Learning.summary: Responses with headers, lists and greater length receive high scores from reward models (RMs), and RLHF policies learn to produce these features even when true quality does not improve. Practitioners therefore edit their RMs, but they learn whether an edit works only after an RL run. We show that the response of a policy to an RM edit can be forecast before training, from samples of the current policy and the scores of the old and new RM. If we read the RM as a set of prices, the first-order theory of KL-regularized RL implies that each feature moves in proportion to its within-prompt covariance with the change in reward. We implant controlled price changes into retrained RMs under a 2^(4-1) fractional factorial design with a self-distilled placebo, run 54 RL runs from six parent policies, and fix every forecast before the runs. With the covariance predictor, we predict the direction of all 20 changes in supply whose forecast has the same sign at every parent and explain 82% of the standardized change. With counterfactual prices, the classical alternative, we explain 50%. The forecast also holds under GRPO and for real RM upgrades, where we explain 66% out of sample with a coefficient frozen from the factorial runs. For rent, the gap between the proxy reward and a gold reward from stronger judges, we rank RM edits correctly with the same covariance over the first 30 steps (Spearman 0.94). This measures the horizon of the forecast: by step 200, the ranking of the factorial edits reverses under both RLOO and GRPO, while the real upgrades keep their order. When we vary the KL coefficient beta, the initial response does not depend on beta, and the response saturates below the KL equilibrium. In one experiment, the long-run response to a price rise is consistent with an additional implicit regularizer beta_0 of about 0.003 to 0.007.

Machine Learning.title: What Structurally Breaks an Agent? Auditing Difficulty in Stateful Tool-Use Workflows
Machine Learning.summary: An aggregate task score does not distinguish failures of scheduling, state retention, and candidate selection. We develop a small executable instrument that varies dependency depth, candidate count, active state width, and access to current-state snapshots while holding the number of required operations fixed. Two dependency-graph families show that increasing depth at fixed work changes both scheduling freedom and the number of reachable completion states, so these controls are coupled, and we quantify the coupling. The primary study contains 49,152 generated tasks and 393,216 reference-controller rollouts. A separately frozen follow-on design adds 295,936 rollouts covering retention strategy, snapshot cadence, hidden state resampling, recovery, query locality, candidate indexing, and relabeling. Residue caches and precomputed plans solve tasks that defeat limited raw-value caches, and indexed selection removes the serial-scan branching deficit. Hidden resampling imposes an exact success ceiling that additional state tracking cannot overcome. The contribution is an executable diagnostic instrument, analytic calibration, and an audit of its assumptions. A small local CPU study with a 0.5B model completed no workflows, and a 16-episode Copilot-routed fractional factorial is descriptive only. Neither supports general capability claims.

Machine Learning.title: CERBO: Certified Recourse at a Requested Rate for Gradient-Boosted Trees
Machine Learning.summary: Recourse-aware learning trains models so that people who receive an adverse decision can reverse it with an affordable change. For gradient-boosted decision trees (GBDTs), the existing method, RABIT, exposes a single recourse weight whose effect on the recourse rate is abrupt and data-dependent, and its training bound cannot certify recourse for any rejected individual. We present Certified Recourse Boosting (CERBO), which takes a requested recourse rate and returns a GBDT with certified actions: it tracks exact additive effort along tree paths, trains against committed boxes (a family of bounds that contains RABIT's and certifies a within-budget action for each training sample) and adjusts the weight after every tree until the certified rate meets the request. A calibration step guarantees the rate on new individuals, and the certifier runs on any tree ensemble, including XGBoost and LightGBM, in milliseconds per person without a solver. In RABIT's own experimental protocol, at equal accuracy, CERBO raises the recourse ratio from 0.90 to 0.99 on FICO and from 0.64 to 0.77 on Bail. Under additive costs on six data sets, it raises the area under the accuracy-recourse frontier in all 12 settings, and in simulated deployments it guarantees recourse to 70% of rejected individuals in 11 of 12 settings, against 2 for RABIT.

Machine Learning.title: NeuralCrop: Combining physics and machine learning for improved crop modelling
Machine Learning.summary: Global gridded crop models (GGCMs) are crucial for projecting climate impacts on agricultural productivity and assessing associated risks to food security. However, state-of-the-art GGCMs are subject to substantial uncertainties arising from reduced representations of complex processes. Projected increases in the frequency and severity of climate extremes require more reliable agricultural yield simulations. Recent machine learning approaches trained on observational data provide alternatives to GGCMs, but remain under-constrained due to sparse observations and show poor out-of-distribution generalization. Here we introduce NeuralCrop, a differentiable hybrid GGCM that combines the strengths of an advanced process-based GGCM (LPJmL) with data-driven components. NeuralCrop is first trained to reproduce its underlying fully process-based version, before it is fine-tuned on observational flux data of physiological variables. Evaluation against held-out flux-tower observations from European wheat and US maize sites shows 32.6-45.2% reductions in mean normalized root-mean-square error for daily carbon and water fluxes. Although fine-tuned only on physiological variables, NeuralCrop improves temporal correlations with independent yield records across 71.4% of the cultivated area for European wheat and 84.0% for the US Corn Belt during 1981-2019. It performs highly competitively compared to GGCMI Phase~3 models. NeuralCrop reproduces yield anomalies more accurately across a range of soil-moisture conditions and especially for extreme drought conditions. For large-scale, long-term simulations, NeuralCrop runs nearly two orders of magnitude faster than the CPU-based LPJmL baseline model, mainly thanks to GPU acceleration. Our results highlight end-to-end hybrid crop modelling as a promising avenue for improving crop simulations and informing food security assessments under climate change.

Machine Learning.title: NIV: Neural Axis Variations for Variable Font Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Variable fonts enable continuous variation of glyph geometry along semantic design axes such as weight, width, slant, and optical size. However, constructing a variable font from a static font remains a labor-intensive process requiring expert typographic design and manual specification of glyph variation data. We introduce NIV (Neural Axis Variations), a method that automatically converts a static font into a fully functional variable font. Given glyph outlines and a set of desired design axes, NIV predicts per-point displacements. The model operates directly on vector glyph geometry and employs a novel Property Embedding mechanism that captures interactions between multiple axes, enabling consistent multi-axis variation within a unified framework. We train NIV on a newly constructed dataset derived from variable Google Fonts, comprising over one million variation tuples. The resulting model generalizes across unseen code points, unseen font styles, high-complexity CJK glyphs, and even out-of-distribution handwriting inputs. The generated outputs are standard variable font files supporting continuous interpolation via existing rendering engines. To facilitate research, we release the dataset, the complete training and inference implementation, and trained models at https://github.com/ndvbd/NIV. Beyond typography, our approach demonstrates how structured geometric objects with continuous parametric variation can be synthesized using neural deformations.

Machine Learning.title: CIS-Transolver: A Cross-layer Incremental-State Neural Operator for Fine-Scale Automotive Aerodynamic Flow Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Neural operators offer an efficient data-driven approach to predicting complex automotive aerodynamic flows. However, spectral bias limits their ability to reconstruct fine-scale flow variations around geometric features such as side mirrors and wheel arches. Reliable assessment of local geometric changes therefore requires models that capture fine spatial detail together with global flow interactions. Inspired by iterative refinement and state evolution, we propose CIS-Transolver, a cross-layer incremental-state neural operator that integrates local multiscale information into global flow modeling. The method extracts local feature variations and encodes them as zeroth- to second-order geometric moments. These encodings are combined with information from earlier layers to form a cross-layer memory. Memory-derived corrections enter the value branch of Physics-Attention, allowing local details to inform global physical-state interactions throughout the network. We systematically evaluate CIS-Transolver on three public automotive aerodynamics benchmarks, ShapeNet-Car, AhmedML, and DrivAerNet++, covering surface pressure fields and volumetric pressure and velocity fields. CIS-Transolver achieves the lowest mean relative L2 error among the evaluated methods for all five prediction metrics across the three benchmarks. Relative error reductions average 8.72% compared with the best baseline for each metric. Also achieves the lowest high-frequency spectral errors across all five metrics, with an average relative reduction of 16.06% compared with the best baseline. These results support cross-layer reuse of local information for fine-scale automotive flow prediction.

Machine Learning.title: CFD-driven symbolic regression of RANS transition models
Machine Learning.summary: Laminar-turbulent transition governs skin friction, heat transfer and losses in turbomachinery, yet Reynolds-averaged Navier-Stokes (RANS) transition models rely on empirical correlations and hand-calibrated activation functions whose structural deficiencies cannot be resolved by recalibration. We propose a CFD-driven sparse symbolic regression framework to learn interpretable, closed-form corrections to the production and destruction activation functions in the intermittency equation of the local, Galilean-invariant $k$-$ω$-$γ$ model of Ge et al. Each correction combines a polynomial of a local pressure-gradient parameter, controlling amplitude and sign, with a bounded exponential of local flow features, controlling spatial support. This construction bounds the corrections without ad hoc limiters. Coefficients are identified by gradient-free optimization with the RANS solver in the loop, accelerated by POD-Kriging field surrogates, using mean-velocity data from wall-resolved large-eddy simulations (LES) of the ERCOFTAC T3 flat-plate cases. Elastic-net hyperparameters are selected automatically through bi-level optimization with leave-one-case-out cross-validation. The resulting model retains 11 of 21 candidate terms, compared with 20 under conventional grid-search tuning, while achieving comparable or slightly better accuracy on training and unseen cases. Both approaches recover the same leading-order correction. Applied without retraining to the transonic LS89 turbine cascade, far beyond the training envelope, the augmented model remains numerically robust and improves heat-transfer predictions at all four operating points, reducing errors by up to 70% where the baseline predicts premature transition under high freestream turbulence. Residual errors in transition onset and length highlight the limits of training on flat-plate data alone.

Machine Learning.title: DynSL: Resource-Adaptive Model Training across Heterogeneous Edge Devices
Machine Learning.summary: Training models over data distributed across edge devices presents a trade-off: centralizing data simplifies training but raises privacy and regulatory concerns, while full local training may exceed the devices' compute and memory capacity. Split learning addresses this challenge by partitioning the model between clients and the server, allowing part of the computation to be offloaded. However, existing approaches typically rely on static split configurations or simplified assumptions that fail to capture the heterogeneity and complex dynamics of real deployments. We present DynSL, a framework that dynamically allocates model layers between clients and the server by continuously monitoring system metrics and periodically solving an optimization problem that accounts for client and server computation and communication. When beneficial, the system reconfigures the split, enabling the offloading strategy to adapt to changing device capabilities and system conditions. Extensive experiments on a testbed of 24 heterogeneous edge devices show that DynSL reduces training time by up to $\sim\!$30% over the strongest adaptive baseline and by more than 50% over a suboptimal uniform split, with no loss -- and sometimes a gain -- in accuracy.
Machine Learning.comment: Accepted at ACM Symposium on Cloud Computing (SoCC '26), Singapore, November 18-20, 2026. Code: https://github.com/BorisRado/dynsl

Machine Learning.title: On the Convergence of Vanilla Adam under Heavy-Tailed Noise and Index Sampling
Machine Learning.summary: Understanding how stochastic gradient noise affects the convergence of Adam is an important problem in stochastic optimization, particularly when the noise exhibits heavy-tailed behavior. In this paper, we investigate the convergence of vanilla Adam in both the expected risk and the empirical risk minimization, focusing on the effects of heavy-tailed noise and its relationship to index sampling. For the expected risk minimization, we establish convergence guarantees under Hölder smoothness and bounded $\mathfrak{p}$-th moment assumptions, allowing stochastic gradient noise with infinite variance. Our analysis provides explicit upper bounds on the expected squared gradient norm and shows that the iteration-dependent convergence term decays more slowly as $\mathfrak{p}$ decreases. For the empirical risk minimization, we establish asymptotic and non-asymptotic convergence guarantees and demonstrate that heavy-tailed population noise can deteriorate convergence bounds through dataset-dependent constants as the dataset size increases. Furthermore, under Lipschitz smoothness, we formulate multistage Adam with practical learning rate schedules and demonstrate that increasing batch sizes can reduce index-sampling noise and improve convergence guarantees and SFO complexity. Numerical experiments support our theoretical findings on the effects of heavy-tailed noise and the computational benefits of increasing batch sizes.

Machine Learning.title: CISA: Retrofitting Dense Attention Models with Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention
Machine Learning.summary: Long-context LLM inference is costly because attention repeatedly reads a growing key-value (KV) history. We introduce Chunk-Indexed Sparse Attention (CISA), which retrofits pretrained dense attention models without gradient updates. CISA selects fixed-size KV chunks using compact summaries of existing keys, avoiding token-level indexing and a separate full-length index cache. It uses one indexing query per KV group and shares selected chunks across queries in that group. During prefill, QShare reuses selections across adjacent queries to reduce indexing cost and improve KV reuse and GPU utilization. We evaluate CISA on NVIDIA Nemotron 3 Nano and Ultra, and Inkling-Small. In one-layer BF16 benchmarks at batch size 32 using Ultra's per-device attention dimensions, core attention is 11.7x faster for prefill queries near the end of a 1M-token prompt and 13.0x faster during decode. Including chunk scoring, selection, and all other measured GPU work, speedups are 8.6x and 3.0x. On Ultra NVFP4 with a 4,096-chunk budget, aggregate scores stay within 1.5 percentage points of dense attention on MRCR, LongBench v2, and GraphWalks. RULER sweeps on Nano and Ultra BF16 up to one million tokens show scores within 2.05 percentage points of dense attention with 8-16x fewer KV reads. Serving million-token prompts with 32 concurrent requests and 4K output tokens per request, CISA achieves 2.29x the end-to-end throughput of dense attention using Nemotron 3 Ultra NVFP4 on four NVIDIA B300 GPUs. Selecting fewer chunks increases throughput to 2.61x; in separate GraphWalks evaluations, the smaller budget widens the aggregate score gap from 1.49 to 3.59 percentage points. These results expose a practical quality-speed tradeoff without sparse training.

Machine Learning.title: Concept-Grounded Reasoning with Prompt-Driven Localization for Interpretable Structured Report Generation
Machine Learning.summary: Medical imaging modalities such as ultrasound and X-ray are widely used in clinical practice, where diagnosis follows a structured, evidence-driven workflow aligned with standardized criteria. While multimodal large language models (MLLMs) show promise for automated medical report generation, most existing systems rely on end-to-end multimodal fusion without modeling clinically defined intermediate attributes, leading to limited grounding and interpretability. To address this issue, we propose CORAL (COncept-grounded ReAsoning with Localization), a multimodal framework that integrates spatial grounding and concept-level supervision into a unified reasoning process. CORAL employs a prompt-driven medical segmentation model to localize lesions and predicts multi-class clinical attributes through a Concept Bottleneck module. The resulting textual concept tokens are combined with mask-modulated visual features within an MLLM to enable structured report generation and diagnostic prediction. Experiments on BUS-CoT and IU X-ray datasets demonstrate consistent improvements in diagnostic accuracy, concept consistency, and report quality over strong general-purpose and medical MLLMs, indicating that concept-grounded reasoning better aligns generation with clinical decision processes.

Machine Learning.title: NashDreamer: Model-Based Reinforcement Learning for Zero-Sum Imperfect-Information Games
Machine Learning.summary: Model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) has achieved remarkable results in single-agent domains, yet its extension to competitive imperfect information games (IIGs) remains underexplored. In multi-agent settings, opponent-induced non-stationarity complicates the learning process, and decentralized model learning faces severe identifiability barriers, which we argue make centralized model learning a mathematical necessity. Building on this analysis, we propose NashDreamer, a principled MBRL framework for two-player zero-sum IIGs. It introduces a centralized Multi-Agent Recurrent State-Space Model (MARSSM) that decouples environment dynamics from the effect of players' strategies on their individual observations. NashDreamer is designed to use arbitrary policy gradient algorithms and inherits their convergence guarantees towards Nash equilibria under an idealized model. Empirical evaluations across five benchmark games demonstrate that NashDreamer substantially improves sample efficiency over model-free baselines early in the training. Finally, we theoretically analyze the architecture's optimization landscape, identifying the vulnerability of the Dreamer family of algorithms to posterior collapse in stochastic environments. We leave it as an open challenge.

Machine Learning.title: Proximal Policy Optimization for Amortized Discrete Sampling
Machine Learning.summary: This paper explores policy gradient algorithms for training stochastic policies to sample from structured discrete probability distributions under the Generative Flow Network (GFlowNet) framework. Building on extensive theoretical connections between GFlowNets and entropy-regularized reinforcement learning, we derive equivalents of standard policy gradient algorithms for training GFlowNets, as well as experimentally explore their various methodological aspects, including baseline training and advantage estimation. Most importantly, our work is the first to derive and successfully apply proximal policy optimization to GFlowNets, showing its improved convergence speed and data efficiency compared to standard GFlowNet training objectives on benchmarks ranging from synthetic energies to molecular graph generation.

Machine Learning.title: ViAdminShift: A Vietnamese Benchmark for Event-Level Knowledge Updates Built from the 2025 Administrative Reform
Machine Learning.summary: On July 1, 2025, Vietnam reduced its 63 provinces to 34, abolished its 696 districts, and replaced its 10,035 commune-level units (wards) with 3,321. ViAdminShift, a Vietnamese language resource about this event, consists of 7,995 benchmark items, 2,281 retrieval passages from pre- and post-reform Wikipedia revisions and dated templates, and old-to-new tables that a released script rebuilds from the official conversion table (not redistributed). Changed items store the pre-reform answer (except 121 address items), a $2\times2$ design uses untouched units as controls, and 400 addresses appear without diacritics. The tables agree with an independent lineage on 10,564 of 10,565 official pairs, disagreements were settled against the resolutions, and the probing-track scorer agrees with both authors' blind labels (Cohen's $κ=0.91$ and $0.89$). Data, outputs, code, and a datasheet are released. In the probing track, at least 20 of 67 models know the reform. Fourteen of them give the new province alone for at most 11% of plain questions about old addresses (old province only: 14-100%); a bare date recovers up to 100%. Post hoc (80 province-free addresses, single runs), with reasoning off, today's date in the system prompt leaves 68-100% old-province-only answers for 10 of 12 models; with reasoning, an "as of" prefix in the question leaves none for seven of eight. On the 1,262-item benchmark subset, with same-source old and new passages, small models unaware of the reform give 14-30% outdated answers and the five benchmark-track knowers (also differing in size or provider) 0-5%.

Machine Learning.title: A Witnessing Duality for ReLU Network Depth
Machine Learning.summary: A depth lower bound for ReLU networks asserts that every sufficiently shallow network fails on some input. What does a proof of such a bound compute? We study this question for exact computation of the maximum of $n$ real inputs, with depth measured by the number of hidden layers. For every separately fixed prime $q$ and depth bound $K$, we give a uniform $\mathsf{TC}^0$ refuter for rational networks with at most $K$ hidden layers and more than $q^K$ inputs, provided that the reduced denominators of their nonbias weights are not divisible by $q$. Biases may be arbitrary rationals. The refuter finds a rational input on which the network fails, and its correctness is provable in $\mathbf{VTC}^0$, the bounded-arithmetic theory of uniform constant-depth threshold computation. The underlying numerical depth lower bound follows from Averkov, Hojny and Merkert (ICLR 2025), extending Haase, Hertrich and Loho (ICLR 2023); our contribution is an internal proof that makes its geometric argument into a feasible refuter. On the construction side, $\mathbf{VTC}^0$ verifies locally checkable certificates for the balanced integer-weight maximum network of depth $\lceil\log_2 n\rceil$. At $q=2$, the construction and refuter meet: for each fixed $K$, the theory verifies that integer-nonbias-weight networks with arbitrary rational biases can compute the maximum with at most $K$ hidden layers exactly when $n\le 2^K$. We also give certified rational constructions of polynomial encoding length and depth $O(\log n/\log\log n)$. These results instantiate a witnessing duality: bounded proofs of certified existence and of refutation correspond, respectively, to threshold-computable constructors and refuters whose guarantees the theory proves.

Machine Learning.title: Causal discovery needs explicit epistemic standards
Machine Learning.summary: There are many causal discovery algorithms, but few guiding principles for choosing between them. Methods are usually compared through three lenses: identifiability, consistency, and benchmarks. Each introduces assumptions about the data-generating process that are often untestable. We argue that there are no shared standards for comparing, prioritizing, or even discussing those assumptions. We support this claim by showing that (i) identifiability assumptions are often preferred by convention rather than by principle, (ii) uniform consistency requires further untestable assumptions, while the weaker pointwise consistency has arguably narrowed algorithm design, and (iii) benchmarks are not neutral tests but carry an epistemic role of their own: they quietly fix which regimes matter, which guarantees come into play, and what counts as success. In doing so, they shape what algorithm comparisons are taken to show and thus perform some of the same epistemic work as theory, but less transparently. In this position paper we argue for a more transparent, integrated practice: Make the epistemic standards for discussing identifiability and consistency assumptions explicit, especially their failure modes and scope conditions; design benchmarks to operationalize those standards, by stress-testing and ablating both. Then, theoretical and empirical results jointly clarify when, why, and how algorithms may work rather than accumulate as disconnected advances.
Machine Learning.comment: This paper was accepted to the position paper track of NeurIPS 2026

Machine Learning.title: LaBraM at Scale: Scaling Data and Models for EEG Pretraining
Machine Learning.summary: LaBraM, an early EEG foundation model, demonstrated that large-scale EEG pretraining can yield strong representations for diverse downstream tasks. Building on this foundation, we expand pretraining data and model capacity while retaining its core encoder and objective. We train ten encoders with 5.8 million to 1.97 billion parameters on three EEG collections spanning 25,067 to 79,910 hours, adapting signal preparation and training to heterogeneous recordings. Across 23 tasks, Atom-L* reaches 59.05% mean balanced accuracy at its best evaluated full fine-tuning (Full-FT) checkpoint, 3.61 percentage points above the strongest baseline EEG foundation model. Quark-G leads linear probing (LP) at 54.33%, a 1.24-point margin. Both also lead average task rank. At the last evaluated checkpoints, larger encoders improve Full-FT more consistently than LP, and stronger LP does not guarantee stronger Full-FT. Preserving patch structure improves LP over average pooling. Data-fraction experiments suggest capacity-dependent saturation, while checkpoint trajectories show that downstream performance can decline as pretraining loss falls. Joint classification with a shared Qwen3 readout reaches 50.50% with Molecule-H and Qwen3-8B; increasing language-model size provides no consistent gain. These results demonstrate the value of scaling LaBraM and the importance of matching pretraining scale to downstream adaptation.

Machine Learning.title: Dissecting Geometric Constraints in Grokking: Interaction-Dependent Acceleration in Modular Arithmetic
Machine Learning.summary: Spherical transformer configurations can accelerate grokking through simultaneous modifications of several model properties. The present study investigated the contributions of these modifications in the published Sphere+Fourier configuration using 960 controlled modular-arithmetic runs. A complete factorial analysis varied residual projection, readout weight normalization, logit scale, and weight decay. Across four matched settings with weight decay, the successful-run mean crossing times without projection were 8-37 times those observed with projection. However, residual projection was insufficient to induce grokking without additional interventions. Various other unprojected configurations also generalized. Since projection altered the magnitude entering the readout, these comparisons could not separate geometry from output scale. A separate 100-run fixed-horizon study demonstrated faster first crossing for the complete configuration across five train/test partitions. Faster crossing did not necessarily correspond to greater persistence over extended training. Control experiments demonstrated rapid grokking without Fourier initialization. Task and depth sweeps also identified conditions in which the configuration failed to reach the criterion by 50K epochs. Accordingly, the observed acceleration depended on interactions among the components and did not extend uniformly across the tested tasks or depths.

Machine Learning.title: PaddleMaterials: An End-to-End Deep Learning Toolkit for Materials Science
Machine Learning.summary: Machine learning supports materials design, atomistic simulation and experimental characterization, yet models and workflows remain fragmented. We present PaddleMaterials, an open-source framework integrating heterogeneous materials-learning tasks while preserving task-specific representations and scientific semantics. It unifies data processing, training, evaluation, pretrained-model management and workflows across six task classes: property prediction, structure generation, machine-learning interatomic potentials, electronic-structure fields, spectrum elucidation and microscopy image processing. Task interfaces record physical quantities, units, aggregation conventions and references, making cross-task composition verifiable. A shared compiler backend enables switching from dynamic-graph to compiled execution through one setting, using graph optimization, operator fusion and hardware-targeted code generation without changing model definitions. Across 65 model instances in 11 groups, compiled execution accelerated every instance in eight groups, with group median speedups of 11%-224% and group maximum speedups of 11%-336%. Case studies on LiMnO2 and toluene link structure generation or spectrum elucidation, interatomic-potential relaxation, property prediction and electron-density prediction, using same-geometry density functional theory (DFT) calculations as references. For LiMnO2, predicted formation energies for generated and relaxed structures differed from same-geometry PBE+U references by at most 7 meV per atom, while the computational cost of model steps was less than one-twentieth of a DFT single-point calculation. PaddleMaterials extends unified materials workflows beyond conventional property, potential and structure-generation tasks while supporting verifiable cross-task operations and compiled execution.

Machine Learning.title: Domain-decomposed Evolutional Deep Neural Network with Random Features for Transient Pressure Diffusion with Discontinuous and High-Contrast Coefficients
Machine Learning.summary: Transient pressure diffusion in heterogeneous porous media becomes difficult to resolve efficiently when permeability is discontinuous and spans several orders of magnitude. In this paper, we develop a domain-decomposed random-feature evolutional deep neural network (DD RF-EDNN) that separates spatial approximation from temporal evolution. Permeability-informed random features are compressed into an orthonormal pressure space, and a conservative finite-volume operator is projected onto this space so that only the reduced coordinates are advanced in time. This formulation retains the dissipative structure of the discrete flow problem without repeated neural-network optimization. The analysis quantifies dictionary and singular-value truncation errors, proves contractivity under an energy-consistent dissipativity correction, and derives a conditional grid-level estimate for homogeneous dynamics and time-independent data admitting a steady lifting. Numerical experiments on low-permeability inclusions, high-conductivity blocks and channels, and three-dimensional grids assess the accuracy of the method across distinct coefficient configurations. The method reaches a final-time relative $L^2$ error of $9.54\times10^{-4}$ in the principal benchmark and maintains errors on the order of $10^{-2}$ at a permeability contrast of $10^3$. Numerical diagnostics further show that the observed error balance and temporal convergence are consistent with the analysis. These results support DD RF-EDNN as a structure-preserving and interpretable reduced formulation for transient simulations on prescribed heterogeneous media.

Machine Learning.title: From PID to Reinforcement Learning in Building HVAC Control: A Control-Architecture Review of Tuning Strategies, Formulations, and Deployment Trade-offs
Machine Learning.summary: This paper reviews control architectures for building heating, ventilation and air-conditioning (HVAC) systems, addressing the tension among energy demand, occupant comfort and equipment operability, and situating proportional-integral-derivative (PID) regulation within a layered control stack that also includes rule-based and model-based supervisory control and data-driven reinforcement learning (RL). It examines the thermostat-PID layer from two-position and scheduled setpoint control through proportional, PI and PID regulation and their tuning, then formulates RL for building control as a Markov decision process. Its central contribution is a taxonomy of where RL meets PID: RL as a gain tuner for an existing loop, as a direct replacement for the regulatory controller, as a hybrid with model predictive control, and as supervisory setpoint and schedule generation. Across these classes, the review establishes that the physical loop remains invariant while the intervention point changes, and that the classes differ in their requirements for actuation authority, state information, modelling, commissioning and constraint handling. It further establishes that PID is inexpensive and well codified but limited by nonlinearity, time variation, discrete mode switching, loop interaction and slow plant dynamics, while RL's admissible position must be argued rather than assumed. The paper concludes that these architectures are not competing philosophies of control but nested points of attachment on one HVAC plant, with hybrid implementations possible, and that deployment trade-offs must be assessed according to the specific control interface and scaffolding required.

Machine Learning.title: FlowBatt: Flow Matching for Probabilistic Battery Degradation Prediction
Machine Learning.summary: Battery degradation remains a central challenge in the development and broad application of sustainable energy technologies. Accurate degradation prediction is challenging, as battery aging emerges from complex and heterogeneous interactions among cycling behavior, operating conditions, and cell chemistry. Existing machine-learning approaches typically focus on deterministic end-of-life predictions or modeling degradation curves within fixed chemistry settings, leaving probabilistic state of health (SOH) trajectory modeling across heterogeneous chemistries underexplored. We introduce FlowBatt, a use-inspired conditional generative framework that adapts flow matching with a diffusion transformer (DiT) backbone to battery degradation trajectory modeling. FlowBatt models full SOH trajectories as probabilistic degradation processes conditioned on early-cycle capacity data. To strengthen this conditioning pathway, we use explainable AI analysis to diagnose and improve the encoder that maps early-cycle capacity matrices into conditioning vectors. We evaluate FlowBatt on five public benchmark settings spanning diverse chemistries and aging conditions, comparing it with supervised and diffusion-based trajectory models as well as established baselines for remaining useful life (RUL) prediction under shared data splits. FlowBatt achieves the best trajectory-wise SOH prediction performance on all five datasets, with errors below 2.5%, and delivers competitive RUL prediction performance. By generating multiple plausible trajectories, FlowBatt provides empirical prediction intervals for battery degradation modeling. These results indicate that flow-matching-based trajectory modeling is a promising framework for probabilistic battery health prediction.
Machine Learning.comment: 29 pages, including references, appendices, and the checklist

Machine Learning.title: Controlling Sharpening in LLM Post-Training
Machine Learning.summary: LLM post-training via reinforcement learning has shown consistent improvements in accuracy at the cost of reducing behavioral coverage - a phenomenon known as sharpening that can stall progress on difficult tasks. Repeated sampling objectives such as $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ are known to mitigate sharpening, but the mechanism behind it remains poorly understood. Moreover, existing approaches for $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization use dedicated algorithms, and no general framework exists for adapting established policy optimization methods from $\mathrm{@}1$ to $\mathrm{@k}$. We derive the optimal policies for KL-regularized $\mathrm{pass@k}$ and $\mathrm{max@k}$ objectives in closed form. Our explicit solutions reveal that $\mathrm{@k}$ optimization naturally redistributes learning pressure based on prompt difficulty, directing it toward harder problems. Crucially, we show that standard $\mathrm{@}1$ objectives achieve these exact same optimal policies through prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation. Ultimately, this yields an optimizer-independent explanation for why $\mathrm{@k}$ objectives reduce sharpening on easy tasks while prioritizing success on harder ones. Building on these insights, we introduce $\mathrm{@k}$ Adaptive Pressure for Policy Optimization (KAPPO). Following a one-time reference calibration, KAPPO seamlessly adapts existing $\mathrm{@}1$ methods to $\mathrm{@k}$ via prompt-adaptive regularization or reward transformation, without otherwise altering their training procedures. Experiments with several RL methods on mathematical reasoning and code generation demonstrate that KAPPO provides direct control over sharpening. Crucially, we demonstrate that $\mathrm{@k}$ pressure can be fully realized with single completion training, matching the performance of multi-completion $\mathrm{@k}$ optimizers at a fraction of the cost.

Machine Learning.title: Entity-Aware Evaluation of OCR Systems for Historical Document Transcription
Machine Learning.summary: Optical Character Recognition (OCR) is essential for digitizing historical archives, yet standard evaluation metrics such as Character Error Rate (CER) do not necessarily reflect whether meaningful information, such as names, dates, and identifiers, is preserved. In this work, we investigate entitylevel analysis of OCR errors as a complementary perspective for evaluating OCR quality in historical documents. Using a publicly available benchmark of 175 documents from the Berrutti Archive, augmented with 5,209 manually annotated entity mentions that will be released upon acceptance, we compare sequence-recognition OCR systems, OCR-specialized vision-language models, and general-purpose vision-language models. Beyond global transcription accuracy, we analyze entity preservation and recoverability under varying character-level edit tolerances. Our experiments show that OCR rankings depend on the evaluation criterion: while Qwen 3.6 achieves the highest entity coverage across all tested tolerances, several systems with lower exact-match coverage recover substantially when small errors are tolerated, suggesting that many of their errors correspond to localized character-level deviations rather than fundamentally incorrect entity transcriptions. Conversely, some systems remain unable to recover many entities even under relaxed matching. These findings show that OCR quality cannot be fully characterized by aggregate transcription metrics alone and highlight the importance of evaluating how OCR errors affect the preservation and recoverability of meaningful information.

Machine Learning.title: The Alignment Illusion: How BadReward Corrupts Text-to-Image Generation
Machine Learning.summary:
Modern text-to-image generative models increasingly rely on Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) to align generated content with human preferences and safety standards. This post-training stage is critical for optimizing models toward high-fidelity and value-aligned behaviors using human preference data. However, while previous works have extensively investigated poisoning attacks against the supervised fine-tuning (SFT) stage of text-to-image training, the security vulnerabilities introduced by the RLHF process remain unexplored.
  In this paper, we present the first exploration into the feasibility of poisoning the RLHF process as a novel attack surface for compromising text-to-image models. We introduce BadReward, an indirect clean-label poisoning attack that manipulates reward signals to embed malicious behaviors. Our approach leverages a feature collision mechanism to produce poison preference image pairs that are visually benign, but aligned with a malicious target concept in the reward feature space. Our experiments demonstrate that this manipulation effectively corrupts the reward signal. Online RLHF further amplifies this corruption through its reward-model feedback loop, whereas offline preference optimization learns directly from the poisoned preferences. Finally, we demonstrate the real-world effectiveness of BadReward on modern text-to-image architectures, showing high attack success rates and visual stealthiness across different RLHF algorithms. Our code is available at https://github.com/ZJUICSR/BadReward.

Machine Learning.title: Guiding Distribution Matching Distillation with Gradient-Based Reinforcement Learning
Machine Learning.summary: Diffusion distillation, exemplified by Distribution Matching Distillation (DMD), has shown great promise in few-step generation but often sacrifices quality for sampling speed. While integrating Reinforcement Learning (RL) into distillation offers potential, a naive fusion of these two objectives relies on suboptimal raw sample evaluation. This sample-based scoring creates inherent conflicts with the distillation trajectory and produces unreliable rewards due to the noisy nature of early-stage generation. To overcome these limitations, we propose GDMD, a novel framework that redefines the reward mechanism by prioritizing distillation gradients over raw pixel outputs as the primary signal for optimization. By reinterpreting the DMD gradients as implicit target tensors, our framework enables existing reward models to directly evaluate the quality of distillation updates. This gradient-level guidance functions as an adaptive weighting that synchronizes the RL policy with the distillation objective, effectively neutralizing optimization divergence. Empirical results show that GDMD sets a new SOTA for few-step generation. Specifically, our 4-step models outperform the quality of their multi-step teacher and substantially exceed previous DMDR results in GenEval and human-preference metrics, exhibiting strong scalability potential.

Machine Learning.title: Inner optimizers in active-learning Kriging reliability analysis: a pre-specified comparison and the unconservative estimates left by unlearned failure modes
Machine Learning.summary: Active-learning Kriging often replaces candidate pools by continuous metaheuristic search. A pre-specified comparison sharing surrogate, population and stopping rule isolated this inner optimizer: five budget-matched continuous optimizers, including hybrid swarm optimization with L-BFGS-B polishing, against candidate pools on eleven problems (dimension 2 to 100). The primary hypothesis was not supported: against optimizers sharing its criterion the hybrid won 6, tied 41 and lost 19 of 66 Holm-corrected accuracy comparisons, and against pool methods 0, 23 and 21 of 44. With sequential selection on three series systems, multistart L-BFGS-B left a failure mode unlearned in 59 of 60 runs, more often than swarm, genetic-algorithm or AK-MCS. In all 198 runs (22 post-freeze) with an unlearned mode, the learned modes did not compensate and failure probability was underestimated (exploratory). The error criterion can accept substantial underestimation: it accepted 17 runs (13 pool-selected) at 0.38 to 0.89 of the reference; 181 exhausted the budget. Follow-up analyses on single-design-point problems indicate underestimation when selections concentrate near the design point. Kriging-believer pool selection satisfied the surrogate stopping criterion with fewer calls than the best continuous method in all four informative batch cells (two post-freeze). We recommend default pool selection and coverage checks for any selection.
Machine Learning.comment: Submitted to Reliability Engineering & System Safety. Full-length version. 4 figures, 9 tables and 3 appendix tables

Machine Learning.title: Preprocessing Choices in Fine-Tuning Data Matter: Utility and Demographic Sensitivity in LLM-Based Recommendation
Machine Learning.summary: Large language models (LLMs) have introduced a generative approach to recommendation, producing item lists from textual representations of user histories and item information. However, this generative setting raises challenges concerning output validity, prompt consistency, and sensitivity to demographic descriptors. In this work, we investigate how preprocessing choices in fine-tuning data affect recommendation utility and fairness-related behavior in a generative LLM-based recommender system. We first establish a controlled recommendation pipeline that combines supervised fine-tuning, catalog-constrained decoding, and prompt augmentation. We then study three preprocessing choices: item-title representation, demographic balancing, and auxiliary item-knowledge enrichment. Experiments on MovieLens-1M show that the catalog-constrained pipeline eliminates out-of-catalog items and ensures complete ten-item outputs, while prompt augmentation improves prompt consistency and utility. Original MovieLens titles increase HR@10 from 10.67% to 12.47% and Coverage@10 from 41.36% to 47.88%. Fairness-related effects are attribute-dependent: age balancing and knowledge enrichment reduce selected group-level utility gaps while largely preserving utility, whereas gender balancing reduces utility without improving the evaluated gender-related indicators. Overall, preprocessing choices in fine-tuning data should be evaluated jointly in terms of utility, output behavior, and demographic sensitivity.
Machine Learning.comment: 11 pages, 2 figures, 5 tables. Accepted at the 3rd Workshop on Evaluating and Applying Recommender Systems with Large Language Models (EARL) at CIKM 2026, November 8, 2026, Rome, Italy

Machine Learning.title: Accelerating Nonlinear MPC by Behavior Cloning with Separated Timescales: Application to Nuclear Reactor Load-Following
Machine Learning.summary: Behavior Cloning (BC) of expert controllers for multiscale dynamical systems is challenging: state variables evolving at widely separated timescales induce highly nonlinear couplings that a shared latent space may fail to adequately represent, degrading closed-loop generalization. We propose Structured Representation Learning for Behavior Cloning (SRLBC), an architecture designed to leverage the physical knowledge of multiscale systems in which slow state variables, fast (stiff) state variables, and predictable exogenous inputs evolve at different timescales. On 500 long-horizon roll-outs of a pressurized water reactor (PWR) load-following benchmark -a high-dimensional, stiff industrial system with challenging safety constraints -and across 20 training seeds, separated embeddings systematically outperform shared embedding baselines on cumulative cost, imitation accuracy and constraint satisfaction. The resulting standalone policies approach NMPC closed-loop performance at a computational cost 15 times lower on average. Since standalone policies still leave a few percent of trajectories infeasible, we embed the learned policies in a safety-augmented approximate NMPC framework, in which the optimizer is only called when the predicted input sequence is not certified as safe. This yields controllers still 6.8 times faster than the NMPC controller on average, with a feasibility (i.e., constraint satisfaction) of at least 99.8% for all architectures, SRLBC retaining the lowest closed-loop cost. Under distribution shift, standalone BC policies degrade sharply: SRLBC degrades the least, and once safety-augmented, it retains a feasibility above 98% with the lowest closed-loop cost. Beyond the quantitative results, Jacobian-based sensitivity analysis shows that the resulting controller relies on a sparse and less redundant set of latent features, each attributable to a single group of physical variables, and aligned with the physical timescale decomposition of the system.

Machine Learning.title: SAT-ACT: Learning CDCL Branching from Outcome-Derived Action Preferences
Machine Learning.summary: Learning-based approaches have increasingly been explored for SAT solving, with particular attention to improving branching decisions in conflict-driven clause learning (CDCL) solvers. These approaches derive branching guidance either from static structural properties of SAT formulas or from dynamic signals obtained through solver feedback and execution traces. However, these forms of supervision provide limited evidence about state-dependent branching effects, while different outcome measures may favor different branching choices. To address these limitations, we propose SAT-ACT, an outcome-derived learning framework for CDCL branching. We design three complementary outcome comparison criteria to extract action preferences from independent branching action rollouts initiated at the same solver state. The criteria identify preferences supported by the outcomes and leave comparisons unresolved when the evidence is insufficient or conflicting, instead of forcing an ordering using a predefined scalar metric. A state-conditioned network learns branching priorities from the extracted preferences and uses them to guide CDCL search directly without online action rollouts. We further introduce non-dominated heuristic action supervision, which retains the solver-selected action as a training target only when it remains non-dominated under these preferences. Solver-level experiments show that SAT-ACT consistently reduces CDCL search costs on three SAT families and improves PAR-2 on the SAT Competition benchmarks.

Machine Learning.title: HandReader: Advanced Techniques for Efficient Fingerspelling Recognition
Machine Learning.summary: Fingerspelling is a significant component of Sign Language (SL), allowing the interpretation of proper names, characterized by fast hand movements during signing. Although previous works on fingerspelling recognition have focused on processing the temporal dimension of videos, there remains room for improving the accuracy of these approaches. This paper introduces HandReader, a group of three architectures designed to address the fingerspelling recognition task. HandReader$_{RGB}$ employs the novel Temporal Shift-Adaptive Module (TSAM) to process RGB features from videos of varying lengths while preserving important sequential information. HandReader$_{KP}$ is built on the proposed Temporal Pose Encoder (TPE) operated on keypoints as tensors. Such keypoints composition in a batch allows the encoder to pass them through 2D and 3D convolution layers, utilizing temporal and spatial information and accumulating keypoints coordinates. We also introduce HandReader_RGB+KP - architecture with a joint encoder to benefit from RGB and keypoint modalities. Each HandReader model possesses distinct advantages and achieves state-of-the-art results on the ChicagoFSWild and ChicagoFSWild+ datasets. Moreover, the models demonstrate high performance on the first open dataset for Russian fingerspelling, Znaki, presented in this paper. The Znaki dataset and HandReader pre-trained models are publicly available.

Machine Learning.title: PDE-SSM: A Spectral State Space Approach to Spatial Mixing in Diffusion Transformers
Machine Learning.summary: The success of vision transformers-especially for generative modeling-is limited by the quadratic cost and weak spatial inductive bias of self-attention. We propose PDE-SSM, a spatial state-space block that replaces attention with a learnable convection-diffusion-reaction partial differential equation. This operator encodes a strong spatial prior by modeling information flow via physically grounded dynamics rather than all-to-all token interactions. Solving the PDE in the Fourier domain yields global coupling with near-linear complexity of $O(N \log N)$, delivering a principled and scalable alternative to attention. We integrate PDE-SSM into a flow-matching generative model to obtain the PDE-based Diffusion Transformer PDE-SSM-DiT. Empirically, PDE-SSM-DiT matches or exceeds the performance of state-of-the-art Diffusion Transformers while substantially reducing compute. Our results show that, analogous to 1D settings where SSMs supplant attention, multi-dimensional PDE operators provide an efficient, inductive-bias-rich foundation for next-generation vision models.

Machine Learning.title: Diagonal Equivalence in State Space Models: Characterization, Retrieval Rank, and Selective Extensions
Machine Learning.summary: We classify real and complex state-space models (SSMs) with linear transitions, distinguishing fixed-basis diagonal equivalence from input-output equivalence and tracking coefficient-conditioning windows under coordinate changes. We characterize diagonal equivalence through commuting transition families whose members are diagonalizable over the chosen field. With time-shared token-local matrix maps, we identify this class's state-mediated kernels with unnormalized scalar-mode linear attention with multiplicative masks. Mamba 3's multiple-input, multiple-output (MIMO) construction lifts one value per local interface; SSD-MIMO routes independent values for local retrieval rank above one. HybridMamba combines Mamba 1's per-coordinate decay, Mamba 2-style heads and Mamba 3's complex rotations and two-endpoint writes, mixing real and rotating state blocks with different decay laws. They recover Mamba 1-3 single-input, single-output (SISO) configurations as exact special cases. On five large H100 bfloat16 workloads, our fused GPU kernels improve geometric-mean training time over official Mamba 1/3 in matched SISO recoveries, with Mamba 2 near parity at SSM-core scope. Memory tradeoffs depend on the baseline and metric: saved-for-backward versus peak allocation. In small-model multi-token recall experiments, both designs outperform Mamba 1-3 on the hardest tier; higher routing ranks perform best in gated or phase-diverse configurations. In single-seed language models with about 500M parameters, both improve on Mamba 1/2 in test loss at 2B tokens, but the routing gains do not translate into lower language-model loss. Our best configurations approach Mamba 3 SISO through 10B tokens while remaining behind it and Mamba 3 MIMO in language-model loss.

Machine Learning.title: Sanity Checks for Sparse Autoencoders: Do SAEs Beat Random Baselines?
Machine Learning.summary: Sparse Autoencoders (SAEs) have emerged as a promising tool for interpreting neural networks by decomposing their activations into sparse sets of human-interpretable features. Recent work has introduced multiple SAE variants and successfully scaled them to frontier models. Despite much excitement, a growing number of negative results in downstream tasks casts doubt on whether SAEs recover meaningful features. To directly investigate this, we perform two complementary evaluations. On a synthetic setup with known ground-truth features, we demonstrate that SAEs recover only $9\%$ of true features despite achieving $71\%$ explained variance, showing that they fail at their core task even when reconstruction is strong. To evaluate SAEs on real activations, we introduce three baselines that constrain SAE feature directions or their activation patterns to random values. Through extensive experiments across multiple SAE architectures, we show that our baselines match fully-trained SAEs in interpretability (0.87 vs 0.90), sparse probing (0.69 vs 0.72), and causal editing (0.73 vs 0.72). Together, these results suggest that SAEs in their current state do not reliably decompose models' internal mechanisms.

Machine Learning.title: An Experimental Study of Hybrid Retrieval, NLI and Open-source LLMs for Scientific Claim Verification
Machine Learning.summary: Claim verification is the task of deciding whether a source text supports a claim, contradicts it, or lacks sufficient evidence. Natural Language Inference (NLI) models can judge whether a single sentence supports or contradicts a claim, but they struggle when the evidence is spread across several sentences. Conversely, Large Language Models (LLMs) can reason across sentences, but may draw conclusions the text does not support. In this experimental study, we test whether a conservative fusion rule, labeling a claim Support or Contradict only when both models agree and defaulting to Not Enough Evidence otherwise, combines their strengths. We construct a benchmark of 2,035 claims from SciFact and CliniFact (858 Support, 152 Contradict, 1,025 Not Enough Evidence). We retrieve the top five most relevant sentences per claim using a hybrid of semantic and lexical (BM25) retrieval, which slightly outperforms either method alone. These retrieved sentences are then provided to every verification model. We then compare a DeBERTa-v3-base-mnli-fever-anli NLI baseline against Llama 3.1 8B, Qwen3 8B, and Mistral 7B. Qwen3 achieves the highest Macro-F1 (0.7937), followed by Llama 3.1 (0.7204) and Mistral (0.6388), while the NLI baseline reaches only 0.3157. Contrary to our hypothesis, fusion degrades performance, dropping Macro-F1 to 0.7392, 0.6730, and 0.5991, respectively. To understand this decline, we analyze agreements, disagreements, and common error patterns between the NLI and LLM verifiers. Our error analysis shows that NLI and LLM disagreements often result in correct LLM predictions being overturned.

Machine Learning.title: The Price of Intelligence: A Quality-Adjusted Price Index for AI Services
Machine Learning.summary: How fast AI inference prices have fallen depends on how an index holds quality constant. We build quality-adjusted price indices for text and code inference sold through APIs, joining 21,024 posted prices to a capability scale fitted to 4,605 benchmark scores. From January 2025 to July 2026, matched-model methods record an annual fall of 0.07 in log price per token. Our pre-specified hedonic index falls at 0.51 a year in logs (95% interval 0.11 to 0.89), entirely through the rising capability of the models on sale. Across three treatments of measurement error and two anchor sets it runs from 0.34 to 0.89. Excluding six anchors flagged for possible contamination leaves model rankings intact (rank correlation 0.998) yet lowers the rate by 0.40 to 0.51 under two treatments. Agreement on rankings therefore does not license claims about levels or increments. Per completed task, the data do not establish a quality-adjusted decline.
Machine Learning.comment: 50 pages, 9 figures. v2 ends the headline window in July 2026, adds three treatments of measurement error and withdraws the per-task result of v1. Accepted (poster), NeurIPS 2026 EconML workshop, non-archival. Data and code: https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22177190; pre-registration: https://doi.org/10.17605/OSF.IO/5UQJ2

Machine Learning.title: Solving Stochastic Inverse Problems in Embedding Space
Machine Learning.summary: Solving an inverse problem consists in finding the unknown parameters of a system from observations. This task is particularly challenging when observations have a strong stochastic component, producing diverse yet equivalent patterns. Self-organizing systems are a notable case: simple local rules can generate complex stochastic patterns. Many natural systems rely on such processes, making self-organization central to understanding natural phenomena. Inverse methods based on direct comparison of observed values struggle in this setting, as such comparisons cannot capture feature similarities between variable outcomes; as a result, the loss fails to meaningfully inform the optimizer. In this work, we show that the difficulty posed by stochasticity in observable patterns can be overcome by reformulating the inverse problem in an embedding space. By mapping stochastic patterns onto an invariant embedding space, where equivalent patterns have similar representations, we can effectively recover unknown causal parameters without the need for handcrafted objective functions or heuristics. We show that embedding models trained on large image datasets produce robust representations that capture these invariances. We evaluate the method on three self-organizing systems: a physical, a biological, and a social one; namely, a reaction-diffusion system, a model of embryonic development, and an agent-based model of social segregation. We show that the method reliably recovers parameters despite stochasticity in the pattern outcomes. We further apply the method to real biological patterns, highlighting its potential as a tool for both theorists and experimentalists to investigate the dynamics underlying complex stochastic pattern formation.

Machine Learning.title: Toward Optimal Regret in Robust Pricing: Decoupling Corruption and Time
Machine Learning.summary: We design the first regret guarantees for robust dynamic pricing that decouple the dependence on the corruption $C$ and the time horizon $T$. In dynamic pricing, a seller with unlimited supply of a good interacts with a stream of buyers over \( T \) rounds, with the goal of maximizing revenue. At each round $t$, the seller posts a price $p_t$, and the buyer purchases the good only if their unknown valuation $v^\star$ exceeds this price. The seller observes only the binary feedback $\mathbb{I} \left\{ p_t \leq v^\star \right\}$, indicating whether a sale occurred. In the \emph{robust} pricing setting, a malicious adversary is allowed to corrupt this feedback in at most $C$ rounds. Even if the learner knows the corruption $C$, the best known regret bound is $\mathcal{O}(C\log\log T)$ by Gupta et al. [2025]. This leaves as an open problem to ``decouple'' the dependence on $C$ and $T$. In this work, we resolve this open problem. In particular, we develop a robust variant of binary search that achieves regret $\mathcal{O}(C+\log T)$ when the corruption $C$ is known and $\mathcal{O}(C+\log^2 T)$ when the corruption is unknown.

Multimedia.title: Lab2Sim: Turning Real-World Experiment Videos into Interactive Virtual Experiments
Multimedia.summary: Science experiment videos demonstrate how experiments are performed, but offer no direct interaction for learners. Turning them into virtual experiments requires not only reproducing the observed apparatus and state changes, but also enforcing the preconditions governing each operation. We introduce Lab2Sim, a benchmark of 218 science experiment videos with evidence-grounded specifications and 11,881 rubric items. To address this task, we propose EduVideo2Code, which extracts experimental procedures hierarchically, encodes them as explicit state machines to guide code generation, and refines the resulting pages through execution-based verification. Experiments show that existing multimodal models readily generate runnable pages but struggle to faithfully reconstruct experimental apparatus. EduVideo2Code consistently improves all four evaluation dimensions across two backbone models, with apparatus fidelity gains of 24.15 points.
Multimedia.comment: 21 pages, 9 figures

Multimedia.title: Efficient Cross-Scale Invertible Hiding Network with Spatial-Frequency Collaboration and Non-Invertible Mechanism
Multimedia.summary: Image hiding aims to conceal image-level messages within cover images at the same resolution. Invertible neural networks (INN)-based image hiding has emerged as an important branch. It treats concealing and revealing as a pair of inverse problems on image domain transformation and uses INN's forward and backward processes to address them. Due to architectural constraints, existing INN-based methods suffer from single-scale and single-domain feature extraction and limited nonlinear representation capability, resulting in inferior image quality. To mitigate these limitations, we propose an efficient cross-scale invertible hiding network with the spatial-frequency collaboration and the non-invertible mechanism, termed CrosInv. CrosInv exploits cross-scale and spatial-frequency collaborative features while enhancing nonlinear representation. Specifically, we introduce a cross-scale invertible module that bijectively maps inputs to cross-scale representations. To effectively integrate spatial and frequency information, the cross-scale invertible module employs pixel shuffle, Haar wavelet transformation, and their inverse operations for scale transformation. Furthermore, a non-invertible cross dense module is integrated to enhance the nonlinearity. Comprehensive experiments verify the effectiveness and superiority of the proposed CrosInv.
Multimedia.comment: Submitted by Junxue Yang, Xin Liao (https://msf-hnu.github.io/)

Multimedia.title: VioTech: Frame-Level Violin Playing Technique Detection with Multi-Scale Mixture-of-Experts
Multimedia.summary: Playing technique is crucial for expressive violin performance, yet few violin technique detection models exist. Current systems mainly rely on note-level pipelines that first estimate note boundaries and then classify techniques. This is especially problematic for bowed string instruments such as the violin, where soft onsets and continuous bow-string interaction render note segmentation unreliable. Here, we propose VioTech, a frame-level violin technique detection framework that predicts techniques directly at 10 ms resolution without explicit note segmentation. To handle the large temporal-scale variation among techniques, VioTech combines a frozen MERT encoder with a multi-scale Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architecture and task-specific routing for tonal, articulation, and legato-related predictions. We also introduce VioTech120, the first manually annotated dataset of violin playing techniques constructed from real solo performance recordings, as well as an accompanying note-labeling user interface. Results demonstrate that VioTech achieved consistent improvements over prior methods and significantly enhanced cross-dataset generalization, establishing a new state-of-the-art in violin technique-aware transcription.
Multimedia.comment: Accepted at the 27th International Society for Music Information Retrieval Conference (ISMIR 2026), Abu Dhabi, UAE

Multimedia.title: Camera-Free Object Discovery and Interaction with GazeTags
Multimedia.summary: We present GazeTags, a camera- and computer-vision-free approach for worn head-gaze object awareness. Our small electronic tags cost roughly \$2 each and can operate for more than a year on a coin cell battery. They work in concert with a user-worn device (smartglasses, hearables, etc.) that periodically emits a focused infrared signal aligned with the user's head direction. Only GazeTags within that narrow head-oriented beam wake and respond, providing their identity and optional payloads such as object state or live sensor readings. By avoiding cameras and computer vision pipelines, our approach is very energy efficient, able to operate continuously even in battery-constrained wearables, and sidesteps non-trivial privacy issues. We describe our hardware design, characterize our system performance and operating tradeoffs, and demonstrate how GazeTags can enable practical gaze-aware environments.
Multimedia.comment: Published at UIST 2026

Multimedia.title: Cassette-Editor: An Agent Harness for Editing Video the Way You Do
Multimedia.summary: Coding agents work in an environment built for them: they read and edit a project, a compiler or a test checks each change automatically and points to the fault, and version control keeps every change in a project that people can review, revert, and continue. Video editing agents lack such an environment; whether an edit is correct shows only in the rendered video, which is costly to inspect and does not point to the decision at fault. Existing systems give the agent either a set of editing operations, which covers only anticipated edits, or a script whose output is a video the user cannot keep editing. We present Cassette-Editor, a complete agent harness for video editing that lets the agent edit the way a person does: knowing what the project allows, seeing what each change affects, and revising from there. It makes the timeline document the agent's action language, in which edits are compositions of typed changes rather than separate tools. A schema check and a rulebook shared with manual editing define what the project allows. An accepted patch commits as one step of the history the user also edits; a rejected one leaves the project unchanged, with each problem located and repair options listed for the next attempt. Reads map source analysis to the frames of the current edit, so the agent can tell what the edit now shows. A parity evaluation shows that every manual action the editor registers, on its test fixtures, can be expressed as an agent patch that reaches the same independently specified document. In a preliminary case study of consecutive revisions to a long documentary rough cut, Cassette-Editor completed more of the judged requests than Codex CLI, which worked from media files without the project, with the same model at similar cost; with a stronger model, under which both completed every request, it used fewer tokens and less time per delivery.
Multimedia.comment: 12 pages, 7 figures, 4 tables. v2: substantially revised, with a new title, rewritten text, and a new evaluation. Preprint; evaluation to be extended in a future version

Multimedia.title: Autoregressive Image Generation with Linear Complexity: A Spatial-Aware Decay Perspective
Multimedia.summary: Autoregressive (AR) models have recently emerged as a promising paradigm for image generation, as they can model visual tokens through the same next-token prediction principle that underlies large language models. However, most competitive AR image generators still rely on Transformer attention, whose quadratic token interaction cost and growing key-value cache become increasingly expensive for high-resolution visual sequences. Linear attention provides an attractive route to efficient AR generation, but our study shows that directly importing linear or decay-based attention from language modeling leads to clear quality degradation. We identify a key cause: after a 2D token map is flattened by raster scan, 1D sequence locality no longer faithfully reflects spatial locality, and conventional decay mechanisms may introduce a false-locality bias at row transitions. To address this problem, we propose Linear Attention with Spatial-Aware Decay (LASAD), a simple recurrent attention mechanism that modulates decay according to the original 2D token geometry while preserving linear complexity. Built upon this layer, LASADGen replaces standard attention in an AR image generator with spatial-aware linear attention.
